title: Andrée's Arctic Balloon
subtitle: Svalbard and the Arctic pack ice · 1897
voice_instructions: Measured, quiet, a little hushed — calm and unhurried, but with a touch more forward energy than a long documentary; the cold voice of something that read the whole file. Never sensational. Small pauses.

beats.vo: This photograph waited thirty-three years in the ice. Nils Strindberg took it in July, eighteen ninety-seven, after their balloon came down.
beats.picture: Nils Strindberg's own photograph of the balloon Örnen down on the pack ice, July 1897: the huge dark half-deflated balloon, the gondola on its side, two small figures standing beside it. One of the frames recovered with the bodies in 1930 and developed then.

beats.vo: Three days earlier, three Swedes lifted off from Svalbard, hoping to fly over the North Pole.
beats.picture: Photograph by Alexis Machuron of the balloon lifting off from Danes Island (Danskøya), Svalbard, 11 July 1897: dark balloon rising over water, mountains behind.

beats.vo: They camped by the wreck a week, then set out on foot for land.
beats.picture: Strindberg photograph of the camp at the landing site on the pack ice, 1897: a tent, the boat, one man standing on a box raising a flag, another man walking away in the foreground.

beats.vo: In October, the drifting ice brought them to White Island. Within days, their diaries stop.
beats.picture: A MODERN photograph (2011) of the rocky shore of Kvitøya (White Island), driftwood, sea ice and fog beyond: near where the last camp was found in 1930.

beats.vo: In nineteen thirty, sealers found their camp, and the men came home to Stockholm. Why they died is still debated: illness from bear meat, cold, or something else.
beats.picture: Photograph from 1930, Stockholm: schoolchildren at an exhibition at Liljevalchs looking at finds from the expedition (the canvas boat's frame in front of them).

facts.claim: The expedition was Swedish: S. A. Andrée, Nils Strindberg and Knut Frænkel, three Swedes, in the hydrogen balloon Örnen (the Eagle), aiming to fly over the North Pole ('three Swedes', 'hoping to fly over the North Pole')

Launch from Danes Island (Danskøya), Svalbard, on 11 July 1897 ('lifted off from Svalbard', 'SVALBARD · 1897'); the B02 photograph (Commons 'Andree.launch.02.png') is credited to Alexis Machuron, dated 1897-07-11
The balloon came down on the pack ice on 14 July 1897, about three days after launch (11 July) ('three days earlier', 'came down on the Arctic ice'; Svalbard Museum: 'after just 65 hours aloft')

Strindberg photographed the balloon after landing (B01 'Örnen omedelbart efter landningen på isflaket den 14 juli 1897'); his exposed film was recovered on Kvitøya in 1930 and developed in Stockholm in 1930 by John Hertzberg (KTH), 33 years after it was taken ('waited thirty-three years in the ice', '33 YEARS IN THE ICE'; Svalbard Museum: 'The films could be developed despite years under ice and snow'; 1930 press: 'Thirty-three-year-old films successfully developed')

They spent about a week at the landing site, then set out on foot over the drifting ice on 22 July toward Franz Josef Land, later toward Sjuøyane ('camped by the wreck a week, then set out on foot for land'; B03 shows the camp at the landing site)

In early October 1897 the drifting ice brought them to Kvitøya (White Island): from 12 September they drifted on a floe toward Kvitøya, the floe broke up on 2 October, and they landed about 5 October; Strindberg's diary ends 7 October and Andrée's 8 October ('Within days, their diaries stop')

Norwegian sealers of the Bratvaag (Gunnar Horn's expedition) found the last camp on Kvitøya on 5 August 1930 (some sources: 6 August); the sealer Isbjørn found more, including the tin box with Strindberg's film, on 5 September 1930 ('Sealers found their camp in nineteen thirty', 'FOUND · 1930')
B05: schoolchildren at a 1930 exhibition of the Kvitøya finds at Liljevalchs konsthall, Stockholm (Wikipedia/Commons caption)

Why all three died is still debated: theories include trichinosis/illness from undercooked polar bear meat (Tryde 1952), hypothermia/cold and exhaustion (Kjellström), and others (vitamin A, carbon monoxide, lead, botulism, scurvy); Svalbard Museum: 'The cause remains a mystery'; National Geographic: 'The causes of the men's deaths are still unknown'

Still unresolved as of 2026: TV4 (2 July 2024) on Bea Uusma's 2024 Kvitøya expedition: 'exakt vad som hände är än idag inte känt'; Karolinska Institutet podcast Medicinvetarna #200 (published 17 June 2026) still frames it as an open mystery ('Inom bara några dagar var alla tre döda'); no definitive finding reported 2024-2026

In 1930 the men's remains were brought home to Stockholm (gunboat Svensksund; funeral from Storkyrkan 5 Oct 1930); the 1930 B05 photo shows schoolchildren at the Liljevalchs exhibition of the finds ('In nineteen thirty, sealers found their camp, and the men came home to Stockholm'; cap 'STOCKHOLM · 1930'; added after blind image check 11-26)
